title: India Is Buying Oil From Venezuela, Brazil, Angola and Nigeria. The Hormuz Shutdown Forced Its Hand.
excerpt: As the Strait of Hormuz enters its fourth month of near-total closure, Indian refiners have quietly built a new supply chain stretching from Latin America to West Africa — a structural shift that may outlast the conflict.
body:
More than four months into the Iran conflict, the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to commercial shipping. For India — the world's third-largest crude oil importer — the disruption has forced a wholesale rewriting of where its oil comes from, how much it costs, and who benefits from the crisis.

Indian refiners have sharply increased crude oil purchases from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria in April and May to cover shortfalls caused by the near-total shutdown of the strait, according to preliminary data from trade intelligence firm Kpler. The shift is no longer a temporary fix. It is beginning to look like a structural realignment of India's energy supply chain.

## The Numbers Behind the Pivot

Before the Iran war erupted in late February, the Strait of Hormuz handled roughly one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. India relied heavily on Gulf producers — Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, and the UAE — for the bulk of its crude imports. That supply line has been strangled.

Kpler data shows India is still receiving approximately 1.9 million barrels per day of Russian oil in May, along with roughly 41,000 bpd from Iraq. But the Middle Eastern share of India's oil basket has collapsed. In its place, Latin American and African producers have stepped in.

Venezuela has emerged as a particularly notable beneficiary. Kpler data indicates the South American producer is on track to become India's fourth-largest oil supplier in May, reflecting surging demand for heavy crude as Gulf flows remain constrained. Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria have also seen increased Indian buying.

## Why India Cannot Wait for Hormuz to Reopen

The urgency is driven by arithmetic. Iranian oil exports fell to their lowest level in six years in May — below 300,000 barrels per day, down from nearly 1.9 million bpd in March — largely due to the U.S. naval blockade enforced since mid-April. The broader disruption to Gulf exports has removed an estimated 710,000 bpd from global markets in May alone, according to Reuters, up from 500,000 bpd in the first month of the conflict.

An average of just three tankers a day has crossed in and out of Hormuz since the fighting began — roughly one-tenth of pre-war volumes, according to shipping monitors including LSEG and Kpler. Nearly 900 outbound tankers have reportedly gone "dark" — switching off their transponders to slip through the strait undetected — while others have paid Iran up to $2 million in transit tolls through Tehran's newly established Persian Gulf Strait Authority.

The U.S. has sanctioned the authority and prohibited shipping companies from striking deals with Iran for safe passage. But some traders and shippers have reportedly done so anyway, desperate to get oil moving to markets where stockpiles are being rapidly depleted.

## The Strategic Calculus

India's government and refiners have framed the diversification as a deliberate strategy, not a panicked reaction. The shift to Latin American and African crude reduces India's exposure to the single chokepoint that has defined its energy vulnerability for decades.

But it comes at a cost. Longer shipping routes from Brazil and West Africa mean higher freight charges, extended delivery times, and a different grade of crude that not every Indian refinery is optimized to process. The economic strain is real, particularly as global crude prices remain elevated. Wood Mackenzie has warned that if the Strait of Hormuz stays closed through year-end, Brent crude could approach $200 a barrel, transforming the energy shock "into a global economic crisis."

For the Indian diaspora, the ripple effects are already visible. Higher fuel prices feed directly into inflation, squeezing household budgets in India and raising the cost of remittance-funded living for families that depend on overseas earnings. India's current account deficit is expected to widen, and the rupee — already at record lows against the dollar — faces continued pressure.

## Diplomacy Has Not Delivered

Prime Minister Modi's recent five-nation European tour was partly driven by the energy emergency. India's new trade pact with Oman is being positioned as a way to bypass the strait entirely, and diplomatic engagement with Venezuela — whose acting president recently flew to Delhi with an oil deal — reflects the government's willingness to explore partnerships it might once have avoided.

But the underlying problem remains unsolved. Iran and the United States have signaled progress toward a tentative agreement to halt the war and reopen the strait, but no deal has been signed. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said this week that talks had not been cut off but no progress had been made. Trump has suggested a breakthrough could come "over the weekend," though no details have been offered.

Until the strait reopens — and even after, given how long it will take for Gulf production and shipping to normalize — India's oil map has been redrawn. The question is no longer whether the diversification is temporary. It is whether it becomes permanent.
